quick.summary: Why a list of observations changes nothing, and how to write one insight.
quick.takeaway: An insight says who, what they need, and why.

beats.line: I shared twelve research observations. The team said, interesting, and changed nothing. Why?
Observations say what happened. An insight says why it matters.
Observation: six people saved the form before finishing it.

board.text: saw: 6 saved the form half done

beats.line: Now ask why. They feared losing their work.
An insight statement has three parts. Who, what they need, and why.
Isn’t the why just my guess?
It starts as one. Check it against what they said and did.
New users need to know their work is safe, because one lost form ends their trust.
That one the team can design for.

quiz.question: Which of these is an insight, not an observation?
options: New users need to know their work is safe, because losing a form ends their trust.
Six people saved the form before finishing.
Four people asked where the save button was.
Sessions lasted eleven minutes on average.
quiz.explanation: An insight names who, what they need and why; the others only report what happened.

quiz.question: An observation and an insight are the same thing.
quiz.explanation: An observation reports what happened. An insight explains the need behind it, so a team can design for it.
